messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 76
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Hotel Manager
  trauma_type: Toxic chemical exposure
  pcl5: 73

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Sensory Distraction: I put on loud music or TV, Thought Monitoring: constantly monitor own thoughts for signs of going crazy, Avoid Event Site: avoid site of the event
  Threat: Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home, Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places, Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
  Memory: Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
  Negative Appraisals: Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body, Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Clinical Vignette: Marcus

Marcus was seventy-six years old when a chemical spill at the Grandview Hotel in downtown Pittsburgh changed the trajectory of his final working years. He had managed the property for eighteen years, knew every inch of its infrastructure, and prided himself on the smooth operation of its systems. On a Tuesday afternoon in March, a contractor had been working in the basement mechanical room, and something had ruptured—a container of industrial-grade cleaning solvent that had been stored improperly for months. Marcus had been in his office two floors up when he smelled it first: a sharp, acrid chemical bite that made his eyes water even before the alarm sounded. He had gone downstairs to investigate, as any manager would, and found himself in a cloud of fumes so thick he could barely see the contractor collapsed on the floor. The smell invaded everything—his clothes, his hair, his lungs. He had dragged the man out, called 911, and spent the next six hours in the emergency department being monitored for chemical inhalation injury. The doctors said he was lucky. His lungs had not been severely damaged. But something else had been.

In the months that followed, Marcus discovered that luck was a matter of perspective. The physical symptoms had largely resolved, but his body had become unreliable in ways that terrified him. His heart would race without warning. His breathing would tighten. Sweat would pour down his back when he was sitting perfectly still. He had come to believe that his own physiology had turned traitor—that it was reacting to dangers that no longer existed, or perhaps dangers he could not perceive but that were nonetheless present. What frightened him most was the certainty that he could no longer trust what his body was telling him. If it was wrong about threat now, how could he ever know when a real threat was approaching? He felt helpless in the face of his own nervous system, unable to stop the cascade of reactions that seized him without warning.

The chemical smell haunted him in fragmented, unpredictable ways. Sometimes he would catch a whiff of something—a cleaning product, a solvent, even certain types of air freshener—and the full emotional intensity of that afternoon would flood through him without any clear image of what had happened. He would simply feel the terror, the suffocation, the sense of being trapped in that basement, though the memory itself remained fractured into disconnected pieces that would not cohere into a narrative he could understand or control. Other times, when he tried to think through what had occurred, he could smell the chemical again, vivid and present, even though he was sitting in his living room miles away from the hotel.

He had stopped going to the Grandview. The building itself had become a place he could not enter. But avoidance had spread like a stain beyond that single location. He felt on guard even inside his own apartment, a one-bedroom in a quiet building where he had lived for six years. Loud sounds—a car horn, a door slamming, even his neighbor's television—sent him into a state of hypervigilance that could last for hours. He had begun to construct a smaller and smaller safe zone: his bedroom, then just his bed with the door locked. He filled the silence with loud music or television, something to drown out the possibility of unexpected noise, something to distract him from the constant monitoring of his own thoughts. He had become obsessed with watching his mind for signs that he was losing it, that the exposure had damaged something neurological, that he was going crazy. Every intrusive thought felt like evidence of deterioration.

His daughter had stopped calling as frequently. His ex-wife had expressed concern, but from a distance. He had taken early retirement from the Grandview six months ago, unable to imagine returning to work, unable to imagine managing a building where danger had proven itself to be real and unpredictable. At seventy-six, he had expected his final years to be a period of earned rest. Instead, he found himself imprisoned in a body that had become his enemy, trapped in a home that offered no real safety, and terrified that there was nothing he could do to prevent the next catastrophe. It was this fear—the absolute conviction that he was helpless—that finally pushed him to call a therapist. He was not sure help was possible, but he was certain that he could not continue as he was.
